guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease, the use of the Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological (CEAP) classification is recommended for clinical audit and research.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease, grading of clinical severity and evaluation of treatment success using the revised Venous Clinical Severity Score (r-VCSS) and the Villalta scale for post-thrombotic syndrome, should be considered for clinical audit and research.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Blomgren et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For diagnosis and treatment planning in patients with suspected or clinically evident chronic venous disease, full lower limb venous duplex ultrasound is recommended as the primary imaging modality.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Metzger et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with suspected supra-inguinal venous obstruction, in addition to full leg duplex assessment, ultrasound of the abdominal and pelvic veins should be considered, as part of the initial assessment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Coelho et al.
rec_text_verbatim: When an intervention is contemplated in patients with suspected supra-inguinal venous obstruction, cross sectional imaging by magnetic resonance venography or computed tomography is recommended in addition to duplex ultrasound assessment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Gagne et al., Lau et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For selected patients with suspected supra-inguinal venous obstruction, where cross sectional diagnostic imaging is inadequate or not available, venography and/or intravascular ultrasound may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Lattimer et al., Lattimer et al., Raju et al., Lattimer et al., Kalodiki et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease, air plethysmography may be considered for quantification of reflux and/or obstruction, in particular when duplex ultrasound results do not reconcile with the clinical findings.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Kahn et al., Araujo et al., Gurdal Karakelle et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with symptomatic chronic venous disease, exercise should be considered to reduce venous symptoms.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Benigni et al., Kakkos et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Unchanged For patients with symptomatic chronic venous disease, elastic compression stockings, exerting a pressure of at least 15 mmHg at the ankle, are recommended to reduce venous symptoms.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Mosti et al., Mosti et al., Mosti et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Unchanged For patients with chronic venous disease and oedema (CEAP clinical class C3), compression treatment, using below knee elastic compression stockings, inelastic bandages or adjustable compression garments, exerting a pressure of 20 – 40 mmHg at the ankle, is recommended to reduce oedema.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Vandongen et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease and lipodermatosclerosis and/or atrophie blanche (CEAP clinical class C4b), using below knee elastic compression stockings, exerting a pressure of 20 – 40 mmHg at the ankle, is recommended to reduce skin induration.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Azirar et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with post-thrombotic syndrome, below knee elastic compression stockings, exerting a pressure of 20 – 40 mmHg at the ankle, should be considered to reduce severity.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Azirar et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with post-thrombotic syndrome, adjuvant intermittent pneumatic compression may be considered to reduce its severity.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Ciapponi et al., Kalus et al., Flota-Cervera et al., Martinez-Zapata et al., Rabe et al., Rabe et al., Pittler et al., Aziz et al., Rabe et al., Kakkos et al., Kakkos et al., Bignamini et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Unchanged For patients with symptomatic chronic venous disease, who are not undergoing interventional treatment, are awaiting intervention, or have persisting symptoms and/or oedema after intervention, medical treatment with venoactive drugs should be considered to reduce venous symptoms and oedema, based on the available evidence for each individual drug.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
ToE
Michaels et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence presenting with symptomatic varicose veins (CEAP clinical class C2s), interventional treatment is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence, presenting with oedema (CEAP clinical class C3), other non-venous causes of oedema should be considered before planning interventional treatment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence, presenting with skin changes as a result of chronic venous disease (CEAP clinical class C4 – C6), interventional treatment of venous incompetence is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence, undergoing treatment using endovenous techniques with or without phlebectomies, the procedures should be performed in the outpatient setting where possible.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence treated by endovenous thermal ablation, ultrasound guided tumescent anaesthesia is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Nandhra et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superﬁcial venous incompetence treated under tumescent anaesthesia, buffered solutions should be considered to reduce peri-procedural pain.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superﬁcial venous incompetence undergoing high ligation/stripping, ultrasound guided tumescent anaesthesia may be considered, as an alternative to general or regional anaesthesia.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hamel-Desnos et al., Gavezzi et al., Bootun et al., Chou et al., Pihlaja et al., Onwudike et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superﬁcial venous incompetence undergoing ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy or endovenous thermal ablation of a saphenous trunk, post- procedural compression treatment should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Huang et al., Bootun et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence undergoing stripping and/or extensive phlebectomies, immediate post-procedural compression treatment is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Huang et al., Chou et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence undergoing intervention, the duration of post-intervention compression, used to minimise post-operative local complications, should be decided on an individual basis.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence undergoing intervention, risk assessment for venous thromboembolism is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: San Norberto et al., Wang et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence undergoing intervention, individualised thromboprophylaxis strategies should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence undergoing treatment of a saphenous trunk, duplex ultrasound surveillance should be considered one to four weeks after treatment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Siribumrungwong et al., Rasmussen et al., Hamann et al., Kheirelseed et al., Brittenden et al., Cao et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with great saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, endovenous thermal ablation is recommended as first choice treatment, in preference to high ligation/stripping and ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Malskat et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with saphenous trunk incompetence undergoing thermal ablation, the selection of the device should be left to the discretion of the treating physician.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Vos et al., Çalik et al., Eroglu et al., Gibson et al., Morrison et al., García-Carpintero et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with great saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, cyanoacrylate adhesive closure should be considered when a non-thermal non-tumescent technique is preferred.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Myers et al., Shadid et al., Venermo et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with saphenous trunk incompetence undergoing treatment, ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy may be considered for treating saphenous trunks with a diameter less than 6 mm.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence treated with foam sclerotherapy, the procedure should be performed under ultrasound guidance.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Lim et al., Dos Santos et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with great saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, catheter directed foam sclerotherapy with or without the use of peri-venous tumescent solution may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Vos et al., Holewijn, Mohamed et al., Vähäaho et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with great saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, mechanochemical ablation may be considered when a non-thermal non-tumescent technique is preferred.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: O'Donnell et al., Hamann et al., Kheirelheid et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with great saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, high ligation/stripping should be considered, if endovenous thermal ablation options are not available.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
de Roos et al.,
Michaels et al.,
Zhang et al.,
Vasquez et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease requiring treatment of varicose tributaries, ambulatory phlebectomy, ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy or a combination of both are recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Abdul-Haqq et al., Kiguchi et al., van Gent et al., Gibson et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease requiring treatment of incompetent perforating veins, endovenous ablation, division or ligation should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Ruckley et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients presenting with reticular veins and/or telangiectasias, duplex ultrasound of lower extremity veins should be performed before treatment, to look for associated incompetent veins.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients presenting with reticular veins and/or telangiectasias, significant associated incompetent veins should be treated first, before considering treatment of smaller veins.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hamel-Desnos et al., Rabe et al., Munia et al., Zhang et al., Parlur et al., Bertanha et al., Ianosi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with reticular veins, where treatment is planned, sclerotherapy is recommended, as the first choice treatment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hamel-Desnos et al., Rabe et al., Munia et al., Zhang et al., Parlur et al., Ianosi et al., Bertanha et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with telangiectasias, where treatment is planned, sclerotherapy should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Munia et al., Parlur et al., Ianosi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with telangiectasias, where treatment is planned, transcutaneous laser should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Doganci et al., Paravastu et al., Boersma et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with small saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, endovenous thermal ablation is recommended in preference to surgery or foam sclerotherapy.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Boersma et al., Lane et al., Garcia-Carpintero et al., Mohamed et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with small saphenous vein incompetence requiring treatment, endovenous non-thermal non-tumescent ablation methods may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Doganci et al., Rodriguez-Acevedo et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with small saphenous vein incompetence treated by endovenous thermal ablation, care should be taken to avoid injury to the sural nerve if cannulation is carried out below midcalf level.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Theivacumar et al., King et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with incompetence of the anterior accessory saphenous vein requiring treatment, endovenous thermal ablation should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Bradbury et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with incompetence of the anterior accessory saphenous vein requiring treatment, ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Vasquez et al., Gibson et al., Watanabe et al., Aherne et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with an incompetent saphenous trunk treated with endovenous thermal or non-thermal ablation, concomitant tributary treatment should be considered, as part of a shared decision process.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim:
New
For most patients with varicose veins, without skin changes related to chronic venous disease, treatment of incompetent lower leg perforating veins is not recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Abdul-Haqq et al., Kiguchi et al., van Gent et al., Gibson et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with advanced skin changes (CEAP clinical class C4b, C5 or C6), with isolated or residual incompetent perforating veins, thought to be significant, treatment may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Bellmunt-Montoya et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence requiring treatment, ambulatory conservative haemodynamic treatment of venous incompetence (CHIVA) may be considered, if performed by physicians experienced in this treatment strategy.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Pittaluga et al., Biemans et al., Richards et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with uncomplicated varicose veins (CEAP clinical class C2) requiring treatment, phlebectomies with preservation of the saphenous trunk (ASVAL) may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Dabbs et al., Woo et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with an incompetent great saphenous vein with a very large truncal diameter (more than 12 mm), endovenous thermal ablation should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
De Roos et al.,
Albernaz et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients presenting with foot and ankle varicose veins, phlebectomy, sclerotherapy, and foot perforating vein ligation may be considered during or after ablation of proximal reflux.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hinchliffe et al., Theivacumar et al., van Groenendaal et al., van Groenendaal et al., Nwaeji et al., Darvall et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with symptomatic recurrent varicose veins due to saphenous trunk incompetence, endovenous thermal ablation or ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy with or without phlebectomy should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hinchliffe et al., van Groenendaal et al., van Groenendaal et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with symptomatic recurrent varicose veins requiring treatment, where endovenous ablation is possible, re-exploration of the groin or popliteal fossa is not recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with symptomatic recurrent varicose veins without truncal incompetence, ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy and/or ambulatory phlebectomy should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Neglen et al., Seager et al., Rossi et al., Williams et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with iliac vein outflow obstruction and severe symptoms/signs, endovascular treatment should be considered, as the first choice treatment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with iliac vein outflow obstruction undergoing endovascular treatment, the use of intravascular ultrasound should be considered to guide treatment.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Dumantepe et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with iliac vein outflow obstruction suffering from a recalcitrant venous ulcer, severe post-thrombotic syndrome, or disabling venous claudication, surgical or hybrid deep venous reconstruction may be considered when endovascular options alone are not appropriate.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with iliac vein outflow obstruction, without severe symptoms, neither endovascular nor surgical interventions are recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients undergoing either endovascular or surgical reconstruction of iliac vein outflow obstruction, duplex ultrasound surveillance is recommended one day and two weeks after the intervention, and at regular intervals thereafter.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with iliac vein outflow obstruction, management by a multidisciplinary team is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Goel et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with extensive axial deep venous incompetence and severe persistent symptoms and signs, where previous management has failed, surgical repair of valvular incompetence may be considered in specialised centres.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
Knipp et al.,
Marston et al.
rec_text_verbatim: In patients with chronic venous disease, caused by combined superficial and deep venous incompetence, treatment of incompetent superficial veins should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
Sessa et al.,
Bergqvist et al.,
Noppeney et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with a popliteal vein aneurysm with thromboembolic complications or those that are saccular, fusiform exceeding 20 mm, or containing thrombus, surgical repair should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: O'Meara et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration without infection, the use of local or systemic antibiotics to improve ulcer healing is not recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active leg ulceration, objective arterial assessment is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: O'Meara et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, compression therapy is recommended to improve ulcer healing.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: O'Meara et al., Dolibog et al., Mosti et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, multilayer or inelastic bandages or adjustable compression garments, exerting a target pressure of at least 40 mmHg at the ankle, are recommended to improve ulcer healing.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Jünger et al., Ashby et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, superimposed elastic compression stockings exerting a target pressure up to 40 mmHg at the ankle should be considered for small and recent onset ulcers.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, with ankle pressure less than 60 mmHg, toe pressure less than 30 mmHg, or ankle brachial index lower than 0.6, sustained compression therapy is not recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Dolibog et al., Alvarez et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, intermittent pneumatic compression should be considered when other compression options are not available, cannot be used, or have failed to promote ulcer healing.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Mosti et al., Stansal et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with a mixed ulcer caused by coexisting arterial and venous disease, modified compression therapy under close clinical supervision, with a compression pressure less than 40 mmHg may be considered, provided the ankle pressure is higher than 60 mmHg.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Clarke-Moloney et al., Milic et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with healed venous leg ulceration, long term compression therapy should be considered to reduce the risk of ulcer recurrence.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Gohel et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration and superficial venous incompetence, early endovenous ablation is recommended to accelerate ulcer healing.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Gohel et al., Gohel et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence and healed venous leg ulceration, treatment of the incompetent veins is recommended to reduce the risk of ulcer recurrence.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Bush et al., Bush et al., Kamhawy et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, ablation of the sub-ulcer venous plexus using ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy should be considered as part of the treatment strategy.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Gohel et al., Gohel et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with superficial venous incompetence and active or healed venous leg ulceration, treatment of incompetent superficial veins is recommended, even in the presence of deep venous incompetence.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Abdul-Haqq et al., van Gent et al., Gibson et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration as a result of superficial venous incompetence and perforating vein incompetence close to the ulcer, concomitant treatment of both truncal reflux and incompetent perforators may be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Raju et al., Yin et al., Williams et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active or healed venous leg ulceration and iliac vein outflow obstruction, venous stenting should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Coleridge-Smith et al., Jull et al., Scallon et al., Wu et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with active venous leg ulceration, micronised purified flavonoid fraction, hydroxyethylrutosides, pentoxifylline, or sulodexide should be considered, as an adjunct to compression and local wound care to improve ulcer healing.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Park et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For female patients with pelvic pain and a clinical suspicion of pelvic venous disorders, exclusion of other causes of pain is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Labropoulos et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients presenting with symptomatic varicose veins where there may be a pelvic origin, specific duplex ultrasound assessment of pelvic escape points is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Park et al., Steenbeek et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For female patients with suspected pelvic venous disorders, abdominal and/or transvaginal ultrasound should be considered to confirm the presence of venous pathology.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Creton et al, Castenmiller et al., Hartung et al., Gavrilov et al., Delfrate et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with varicose veins of pelvic origin without pelvic symptoms requiring treatment, local procedures for varicose veins and related pelvic escape points should be considered, as initial therapeutic approach.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Creton et al., Castenmiller et al., Hartung et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with varicose veins of pelvic origin without pelvic symptoms, pelvic vein embolisation as initial treatment should not be performed.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Hartung et al., Champaneria et al., Brown et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with varicose veins of pelvic origin with pelvic symptoms requiring treatment, pelvic vein embolisation should be considered to reduce symptoms.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: For patients who have had acute spontaneous bleeding from superficial veins, referral for urgent assessment and treatment is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
Hamahata et al,
Serra et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease who have suffered from an episode of acute bleeding of superficial veins or telangiectasias, local foam sclerotherapy should be considered to prevent recurrent bleeding.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
Parkyn et al.,
Shaalan et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease, who are obese, weight loss should be considered for improving venous outcomes.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Deol et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For obese patients with saphenous trunk incompetence requiring treatment, endovenous ablation should be considered.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors:
Thaler et al.,
Adamczyk et al.,
Saliba et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For pregnant women presenting with symptoms and/or signs of chronic venous disease, the use of elastic compression hosiery is recommended.

guideline_name: Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs
evidence_first_authors: Westin et al.
rec_text_verbatim: For patients with chronic venous disease, who are on anticoagulants and scheduled to undergo endovenous thermal ablation, interruption of anticoagulation is not recommended.
